title: Rethinking Expressivity and Efficiency in Test-Time Training

paper.title: Rethinking Expressivity and Efficiency in Test-Time Training
paper.abstract:
Abstract Test-Time Training (TTT) enables long-context processing via continuous weight updates during inference, but current methods struggle to balance the expressivity of per-token update dynamics with the hardware efficiency of chunk-wise approximations. We propose E 2 -TTT (Expressive and Efficient TTT) to bridge this gap.

Under the standard approximation of taking gradients at the chunk-start weights, we derive a closed-form state transition that exactly reproduces the chunk-end fast-weight and momentum states of the per-token recurrence.

This enables fully parallelized chunk-level training while preserving the temporal structure of the update rule that prior chunk-wise methods discard.
We validate E 2 -TTT by training models up to 1.3B parameters from scratch.

It performs on par with previous TTT and hybrid attention baselines in language modeling while outperforming them on in-context retrieval. Its advantage is most pronounced in length extrapolation: on the standard “Needle in a Haystack” passkey test, it retains over 90% accuracy at 8 × 8\times the training context length.

Meanwhile, E 2 -TTT can match the training throughput of efficient chunk-wise methods, demonstrating that it effectively reconciles expressivity with efficiency.
The code is available at https://github.com/zeyun-zhong/E2-TTT .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: State-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) [ 44 , 16 , 2 ] demonstrate remarkable capabilities in reasoning, coding, and multimodal understanding. However, once trained, the weights of these models remain frozen, leaving them to rely solely on accumulated memory, e.g. , key-value cache [ 48 , 49 ] , for processing long-context agentic tasks [ 43 , 41 , 34 ] . This fundamental limitation hinders their ability to continuously learn from long-horizon tasks or generalize across tasks in real-world scenarios. Two primary approaches have emerged to address this limitation. The first seeks to reduce the computational complexity of attention from quadratic to linear by introducing RNN-style or hybrid architectures [ 13 , 64 , 47 , 32 ] , thereby enabling the processing of longer sequences. However, as demonstrated in Tandon et al. [58] , these techniques still remain less effective than full attention in long-context language modeling. The second approach, known as Test-Time Training [ 56 , 9 ] , extends the concept of recurrent states to small, online-adapted sub-networks ( e.g. , fast weights [ 54 ] ), allowing models to continuously adapt their parameters during inference. Numerous recent studies [ 12 , 58 , 69 ] have explored its potential for long-context text and multimodal tasks. Despite their promise, existing TTT methods face a well-known dilemma between expressivity and efficiency. On the one hand, vanilla TTT [ 56 , 9 ] adopts token-wise updates, which offer powerful expressiveness but result in slow training, as token-level dependencies enforce sequential recurrence. On the other hand, chunk-wise TTT [ 69 ] substantially improves efficiency by executing updates over larger chunks, yet it sacrifices expressivity due to oversimplifications of the update rule, effectively obscuring the temporal variance of token importance within a chunk. To achieve the best of both worlds in expressivity and efficiency, we propose E 2 -TTT, a novel TTT approach that reconciles token-level expressiveness with chunk-level computational efficiency. The core innovation is a closed-form parallel scalar kernel that enables parallel execution of recurrent dynamics with per-token learning rate, momentum, and decay. Specifically, our formulation preserves the exact per-token effect on the chunk-end fast-weight state, a temporal structure that prior chunk-wise methods discard via averaging, while retaining chunk-level hardware parallelism. Furthermore, we integrate E 2 -TTT into a hybrid architecture that combines TTT with sliding window attention, enabling our model to handle long-horizon tasks while maintaining fine-grained local context. We empirically validate E 2 -TTT by training models of up to 1.3B parameters from scratch on 15B tokens from the HuggingFace FineWeb-Edu dataset [ 46 ] , comparing against strong linear attention and hybrid baselines. Our evaluation spans general language modeling, in-context retrieval, and length extrapolation, where the gains concentrate in the retrieval and extrapolation regimes. Notably, our model exhibits strong robustness in length extrapolation, maintaining > 90 % >90\% accuracy on passkey retrieval in the standard “Needle in a Haystack” test at 8 × 8\times the training context, a regime where prior chunk-based methods collapse. Finally, we explore the versatility of our approach through parameter-efficient adaptation for long-context video understanding, achieving performance comparable to full fine-tuning at the 2B-parameter scale on standard multimodal benchmarks. Overall, we demonstrate the benefit of expressive sequential updates while matching the training throughput of standard chunk-wise TTT, offering novel insights into the TTT paradigm.

sections.heading: 3 Expressive and Efficient Test-Time Training
sections.text: Current TTT variants present a stark trade-off: token-wise updates offer high optimization fidelity but suffer from sequential bottlenecks, while chunk-wise updates achieve hardware efficiency by simplifying the update rule, effectively obscuring the temporal variance of token importance within a chunk. To resolve this dichotomy, we introduce E 2 -TTT (Expressive and Efficient TTT). Our key contribution is a novel theoretical formulation that maps a token-wise recurrence with coupled momentum and decay into a closed-form, chunk-parallel update, reproducing its chunk-end states without approximating the per-token dynamics. This allows us to retain the precise per-token temporal weighting of each gradient contribution while matching the hardware efficiency of coarse-grained chunk processing. Table 1 summarizes this advantage. For simplicity, we omit the chunk indices r r in this section ( e.g. 𝐖 t = 𝐖 t [ r ] \mathbf{W}_{t}=\mathbf{W}^{[r]}_{t} ). We index steps within a chunk as t ∈ { 1 , … , C } t\in\{1,\dots,C\} , where t = 0 t=0 denotes the state inherited from the previous chunk ( 𝐖 0 = 𝐖 C [ r − 1 ] \mathbf{W}_{0}=\mathbf{W}^{[r-1]}_{C} , 𝐌 0 = 𝐌 C [ r − 1 ] \mathbf{M}_{0}=\mathbf{M}^{[r-1]}_{C} ).

sections.heading: 4 E 2 -TTT Model Architecture
sections.text: The design of our architecture is driven by a specific characteristic of chunk-wise processing: the output step (Eq. 6 ) applies a fixed state to the entire chunk. This renders the TTT path “blind” to the immediate causal history within the current chunk (i.e., token 𝒙 t [ r ] \bm{x}_{t}^{[r]} cannot influence the processing of 𝒙 t + 1 [ r ] \bm{x}_{t+1}^{[r]} via the fast weights). To address this, we adopt the proven hybrid design pattern in prior work [ 3 , 26 , 42 , 69 ] , pairing our E 2 -TTT module (for modeling non-local dependencies) with a standard Sliding Window Attention module (for capturing local dependencies), as shown in Fig. 2 . Overall Architecture. The macro-architecture of E 2 -TTT follows the standard Llama design [ 59 ] , interleaving token mixing layers with SwiGLU MLP blocks. Given an input sequence 𝐗 ∈ ℝ L × d \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} , we first project it into shared queries 𝐐 \mathbf{Q} , keys 𝐊 \mathbf{K} , and values 𝐕 \mathbf{V} . These are fed into two parallel processing branches: a Sliding Window Attention (SWA) module for local retrieval, and our E 2 -TTT layer for long-range context modeling. For the TTT path, we follow [ 28 , 69 ] by applying SiLU activation to the queries and keys, followed by L2 normalization to ensure training stability. Simultaneously, the scalars required for the TTT update rule are predicted by the network directly: the learning rate η t \eta_{t} , momentum β t \beta_{t} , and decay strength α t \alpha_{t} are projected directly from 𝐗 \mathbf{X} via lightweight linear heads, while the final decay factor γ t \gamma_{t} is derived from η t \eta_{t} and α t \alpha_{t} . To combine the complementary strengths of both branches, we adopt a dynamic mixing strategy [ 28 ] : the outputs are fused via element-wise interpolation, controlled by a data-dependent gate projected from the input 𝐗 \mathbf{X} . Finally, the fused output is normalized and processed through the output projection. Figure 2 : E 2 -TTT token mixing block. SWA and E 2 -TTT run in parallel over shared 𝐐 , 𝐊 , 𝐕 \mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V} and are fused by a data-dependent gate. The TTT update is modulated by input-dependent α , η , β \alpha,\eta,\beta . Input-Dependent Dynamics. To allow the model to modulate its learning dynamics at the token level, we parameterize the update coefficients η t , β t , γ t \eta_{t},\beta_{t},\gamma_{t} as functions of the input 𝒙 t ∈ ℝ d \bm{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . We adopt standard parameterization schemes from prior TTT and linear attention literature to ensure stability and effective long-term retention. The corresponding linear projections are learned end-to-end from the language-modeling loss alone, without auxiliary objectives. Specific base scalars are detailed in Appendix B.1 . Performance is empirically robust to these base scalars across an order of magnitude (Appendix B.3 ). Appendix B.4 further analyzes the coefficients learned by these projections. The learning rate η t \eta_{t} modulates the update magnitude. We parameterize it as a sigmoid-gated value scaled by a base learning rate η base \eta_{\text{base}} [ 56 ] : η t = η base ⋅ σ ⁡ ( Linear η ​ ( 𝒙 t ) ) . \eta_{t}=\eta_{\text{base}}\cdot\sigma(\text{Linear}_{\eta}(\bm{x}_{t})). (12) The momentum factor β t \beta_{t} determines the persistence of historical gradients. To encourage long-term memory retention, we bias the momentum towards values close to 1 1 using a timescale factor τ \tau [ 65 , 57 ] : β t = σ ​ ( Linear β ​ ( 𝒙 t ) ) 1 τ . \beta_{t}=\sigma(\text{Linear}_{\beta}(\bm{x}_{t}))^{\frac{1}{\tau}}. (13) The decay factor γ t \gamma_{t} serves as a forget gate. To prevent excessive regularization when the update step is small, we derive γ t \gamma_{t} from a dynamic decay strength α t \alpha_{t} (scaled by α base \alpha_{\text{base}} ) coupled with the learning rate η t \eta_{t} , consistent with standard optimization practices [ 39 ] : α t = α base ⋅ σ ⁡ ( Linear α ​ ( 𝒙 t ) ) , γ t = 1 − η t ​ α t . \alpha_{t}=\alpha_{\text{base}}\cdot\sigma(\text{Linear}_{\alpha}(\bm{x}_{t})),\quad\gamma_{t}=1-\eta_{t}\alpha_{t}. sections.text: In Table 2 , we present the language modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy on commonsense reasoning benchmarks for models with 340M and 1.3B parameters. sections.heading: 5.3 Evaluating Length Extrapolation Capabilities
sections.text: A critical advantage of our E 2 -TTT is its potential to generalize to sequence lengths significantly exceeding the training horizon. We evaluate this capability across three dimensions: language modeling stability, synthetic long-context retrieval, and real-world long-context benchmarks. Language Modeling Extrapolation. We first assess whether the models can maintain stable language modeling performance when processing sequences longer than their training context (2K tokens). Figure 3 visualizes the per-token loss metric [ 63 ] on six long-context datasets. As shown in Fig. 3 , LaCT struggles with length extrapolation, with loss exploding immediately past the training boundary on all six datasets. HQLT maintains stability but shows higher validation loss (e.g., on CodeParrot). In contrast, both E 2 -TTT variants demonstrate lower and stable loss curves throughout the extrapolated region. This confirms that our expressive chunk-wise updates robustly generalize to unseen lengths. Figure 4 : Zero-shot accuracy on S-NIAH-1 and S-NIAH-2 for 1.3B models. All methods use sliding window attention with a 512-token window. E 2 -TTT maintains robust retrieval well beyond the training context, while LaCT collapses past 4K and HQLT degrades steadily across both tasks. Long-range Associative Recall. Stability alone does not guarantee information retention. To test effective capacity, we employ the “Single-Needle in a Haystack” (S-NIAH) benchmark [ 24 ] , extending the test sequence up to 16K tokens (8 × \times the training horizon). Figure 4 reveals a stark contrast in extrapolation behavior. On S-NIAH-1, both E 2 -TTT variants retain at least 85% accuracy at 16K, while LaCT collapses to near-zero and HQLT degrades to 25%. On S-NIAH-2, E 2 -TTT SwiGLU \text{E${}^{2}$-TTT}_{\text{SwiGLU}} retains a clear lead through 16K, achieving 40.6% at 8K versus 15.4% (HQLT) and 5.6% (LaCT). The SwiGLU variant consistently outperforms the MLP variant in the extrapolation regime, validating the benefit of gated updates for handling complex retrieval patterns. sections.heading: 6 Related Work
sections.text: Test-Time Training (TTT) [ 56 ] is an emerging paradigm in sequence modeling that redefines the recurrent states in RNNs as learnable weights of an online-adapted non-linear neural network. These weights, often referred to as fast weights [ 54 ] , are continuously updated to learn in-context. Existing methods typically employ a self-supervised loss that encourages these fast weights to memorize key-value associations from in-context tokens, effectively treating inference as an online learning problem using variants of gradient descent. While TTT [ 56 , 61 ] has opened a vast design space for novel recurrent model architectures [ 9 , 30 , 8 , 58 ] , the resulting sequential bottleneck leads to poor hardware utilization, limiting their scalability. Recent efforts like LaCT [ 69 ] have attempted to mitigate this by shifting from token-wise to chunk-wise updates, sacrificing intra-chunk dependency modeling to improve throughput. However, these methods often resort to simplified aggregation rules (e.g., flat averaging) that degrade the optimization fidelity. Our work builds upon this foundation but distinguishes itself by introducing E 2 -TTT (Expressive and Efficient TTT), a formulation that reconciles the hardware efficiency of chunking with the mathematical precision of complex, token-wise update dynamics. Combining global recurrence with local attention is a proven strategy for efficient long-context modeling [ 36 , 52 , 15 ] . Following recent work [ 28 , 69 ] , we adopt a within-layer hybrid architecture that shares the key, value, and query vectors between local attention and global recurrence. This design pattern has been successfully deployed in various forms [ 26 , 42 , 5 ] . However, prior instantiations typically rely on standard linear attention [ 31 , 54 , 66 , 28 ] or simplified TTT update rules [ 69 ] . Our work retains this established architectural template but replaces the recurrence module with our E 2 -TTT, empirically showing superior results.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented E 2 -TTT (Expressive and Efficient TTT), a method that reconciles the hardware efficiency of chunk-wise processing with the per-token expressivity of the update rule in Test-Time Training. By deriving a closed-form scalar kernel, we enabled the parallel execution of per-token recurrent dynamics without the chunk-level approximations of prior chunk-wise methods. Empirically, E 2 -TTT is on par with strong sub-quadratic baselines in language modeling and outperforms them on retrieval while demonstrating superior length extrapolation, sustaining > 90 % >90\% passkey retrieval accuracy on “Needle in a Haystack” at 8 × 8\times the training context length, where baseline methods collapse. These results suggest that preserving precise temporal dynamics is essential for long-context generalization, positioning E 2 -TTT as a promising direction for scalable Test-Time Training.

sections.heading: Appendix A Detailed Derivation of the Parallel Kernel
sections.text: In this section, we derive the closed-form expansion of the TTT update rule within a single chunk of length C C . This formulation allows us to “jump” directly from the start of the chunk ( t = 0 t=0 ) to the end ( t = C t=C ) without materializing intermediate states. The chunk index r r is omitted for simplicity. Recall that we consider general per-token updates with coupled L2 decay and momentum. Let the fast weights 𝐖 t ∈ ℝ d × d \mathbf{W}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} , momentum 𝐌 t ∈ ℝ d × d \mathbf{M}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} , and update direction (negative gradient) 𝐆 t ∈ ℝ d × d \mathbf{G}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be matrix-valued. Let γ t , β t ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \gamma_{t},\beta_{t}\in(0,1) be the scalar decay and momentum factors, and η t > 0 \eta_{t}>0 be the learning rate. The recurrence is: 𝐌 t = β t ​ 𝐌 t − 1 + η t ​ 𝐆 t , 𝐖 t = γ t ​ 𝐖 t − 1 + 𝐌 t . \mathbf{M}_{t}=\beta_{t}\,\mathbf{M}_{t-1}+\eta_{t}\,\mathbf{G}_{t},\qquad\mathbf{W}_{t}=\gamma_{t}\,\mathbf{W}_{t-1}+\mathbf{M}_{t}. (17)

sections.heading: A.1 Unrolling Momentum and Weights
sections.text: Unrolling the momentum. By induction, the momentum 𝐌 t \mathbf{M}_{t} at step t t is the sum of the decayed initial momentum at the chunk start and the history of gradients: 𝐌 t = ( ∏ i = 1 t β i ) ​ 𝐌 0 + ∑ j = 1 t ( η j ​ 𝐆 j ​ ∏ i = j + 1 t β i ) . \mathbf{M}_{t}=\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{t}\beta_{i}\Big)\mathbf{M}_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{t}\Big(\eta_{j}\,\mathbf{G}_{j}\prod_{i=j+1}^{t}\beta_{i}\Big). (18) Unrolling the Weights. Similarly, unrolling the weight update (Eq. 17 ) yields: 𝐖 t = ( ∏ i = 1 t γ i ) ​ 𝐖 0 + ∑ j = 1 t ( 𝐌 j ​ ∏ i = j + 1 t γ i ) . \displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{t}=\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{t}\gamma_{i}\Big)\mathbf{W}_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{t}\Big(\mathbf{M}_{j}\prod_{i=j+1}^{t}\gamma_{i}\Big). (19) Insert ( 18 ) into ( 19 ) and separate the 𝐌 0 \mathbf{M}_{0} and gradient parts: 𝐖 t = ( ∏ i = 1 t γ i ) ​ 𝐖 0 ⏟ Decay term + ∑ j = 1 t ( ( ∏ i = 1 j β i ) ​ 𝐌 0 ​ ∏ q = j + 1 t γ q ) ⏟ Momentum term + ∑ j = 1 t ∑ k = 1 j ( η k ​ 𝐆 k ​ ∏ i = k + 1 j β i ​ ∏ q = j + 1 t γ q ) ⏟ Gradient term . \mathbf{W}_{t}=\underbrace{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{t}\gamma_{i}\Big)\mathbf{W}_{0}}_{\text{Decay term}}+\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{t}\Big(\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{j}\beta_{i}\Big)\mathbf{M}_{0}\prod_{q=j+1}^{t}\gamma_{q}\Big)}_{\text{Momentum term}}+\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{t}\sum_{k=1}^{j}\Big(\eta_{k}\mathbf{G}_{k}\prod_{i=k+1}^{j}\beta_{i}\prod_{q=j+1}^{t}\gamma_{q}\Big)}_{\text{Gradient term}}. (20) Re-indexing the gradient contribution. Swap the order of summation in the last term of ( 20 ) by fixing the gradient index k k and summing over j = k , … , t j=k,\dots,t : ∑ j = 1 t ∑ k = 1 j ( η k ​ 𝐆 k ​ ∏ i = k + 1 j β i ​ ∏ q = j + 1 t γ q ) = ∑ k = 1 t η k ​ 𝐆 k ​ ∑ j = k t ( ∏ i = k + 1 j β i ​ ∏ q = j + 1 t γ q ) . \sum_{j=1}^{t}\sum_{k=1}^{j}\Big(\eta_{k}\mathbf{G}_{k}\prod_{i=k+1}^{j}\beta_{i}\prod_{q=j+1}^{t}\gamma_{q}\Big)=\sum_{k=1}^{t}\eta_{k}\mathbf{G}_{k}\sum_{j=k}^{t}\Big(\prod_{i=k+1}^{j}\beta_{i}\prod_{q=j+1}^{t}\gamma_{q}\Big). (21) This converts Eq. 20 to: 𝐖 t = ( ∏ i = 1 t γ i ) ​ 𝐖 0 ⏟ Decay term + ∑ j = 1 t ( ( ∏ i = 1 j β i ) ​ 𝐌 0 ​ ∏ q = j + 1 t γ q ) ⏟ Momentum term + ∑ k = 1 t η k ​ 𝐆 k ​ ∑ j = k t ( ∏ i = k + 1 j β i ​ ∏ q = j + 1 t γ q ) ⏟ Gradient term . \mathbf{W}_{t}=\underbrace{\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{t}\gamma_{i}\Big)\mathbf{W}_{0}}_{\text{Decay term}}+\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{t}\Big(\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{j}\beta_{i}\Big)\mathbf{M}_{0}\prod_{q=j+1}^{t}\gamma_{q}\Big)}_{\text{Momentum term}}+\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{t}\eta_{k}\mathbf{G}_{k}\sum_{j=k}^{t}\Big(\prod_{i=k+1}^{j}\beta_{i}\prod_{q=j+1}^{t}\gamma_{q}\Big)}_{\text{Gradient term}}. (22)

sections.heading: A.2 Closed form at the final step per chunk ( t = C t=C )
sections.text: To efficiently compute the final state 𝐖 C \mathbf{W}_{C} , we define three auxiliary scalar sequences. Let the suffix products for decay γ \gamma and momentum β \beta be: β ~ t := ∏ i = t + 1 C β i , γ ~ t := ∏ i = t + 1 C γ i , \tilde{\beta}_{t}:=\prod_{i=t+1}^{C}\beta_{i},\qquad\tilde{\gamma}_{t}:=\prod_{i=t+1}^{C}\gamma_{i}, (23) (with the empty product convention ∏ C + 1 C ( ⋅ ) = 1 \prod_{C+1}^{C}(\cdot)=1 ). We further define the cumulative ratio sum R t R_{t} : R t := ∑ i = t C γ ~ i β ~ i . R_{t}:=\sum_{i=t}^{C}\frac{\tilde{\gamma}_{i}}{\tilde{\beta}_{i}}. (24) Since these terms depend only on the scalars β , γ \beta,\gamma , they can be pre-computed efficiently in parallel (e.g., via log-space cumulative sums). Initial Weight Carry ( carry w \mathrm{carry}_{\mathrm{w}} ). Directly from definition: carry w := ∏ i = 1 C γ i = γ ~ 0 \mathrm{carry}_{\mathrm{w}}:=\prod_{i=1}^{C}\gamma_{i}=\tilde{\gamma}_{0} (25) Initial Momentum Carry ( carry m \mathrm{carry}_{\mathrm{m}} ). We rewrite the prefix product ∏ i = 1 j β i \prod_{i=1}^{j}\beta_{i} as the total product divided by the suffix product: ∏ i = 1 j β i = ( ∏ i = 1 C β i ) / β ~ j . \prod_{i=1}^{j}\beta_{i}=\big(\prod_{i=1}^{C}\beta_{i}\big)\big/\tilde{\beta}_{j}. (26) Substituting this into the 𝐌 0 \mathbf{M}_{0} term in Eq. 22 : ∑ j = 1 C ( ( ∏ i = 1 j β i ) ​ 𝐌 0 ​ γ ~ j ) = ( ∏ i = 1 C β i ) ​ ∑ j = 1 C γ ~ j β ~ j ⏟ = R 1 ​ 𝐌 0 , \sum_{j=1}^{C}\Big(\big(\prod_{i=1}^{j}\beta_{i}\big)\,\mathbf{M}_{0}\,\tilde{\gamma}_{j}\Big)=\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{C}\beta_{i}\Big)\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{C}\frac{\tilde{\gamma}_{j}}{\tilde{\beta}_{j}}}_{=\,R_{1}}\,\mathbf{M}_{0}, (27) with carry m := β ~ 0 ​ R 1 . \mathrm{carry}_{\mathrm{m}}:=\tilde{\beta}_{0}R_{1}. (28) Gradient contributions. From ( 21 ) at t = C t=C , each 𝐆 k \mathbf{G}_{k} is weighted by the scalar ∑ j = k C ( ∏ i = k + 1 j β i ​ ∏ q = j + 1 C γ q ) = β ~ k ​ ∑ j = k C γ ~ j β ~ j = β ~ k ​ R k . \sum_{j=k}^{C}\Big(\prod_{i=k+1}^{j}\beta_{i}\prod_{q=j+1}^{C}\gamma_{q}\Big)=\tilde{\beta}_{k}\sum_{j=k}^{C}\frac{\tilde{\gamma}_{j}}{\tilde{\beta}_{j}}=\tilde{\beta}_{k}R_{k}. (29) Closed form for 𝐖 C \mathbf{W}_{C} . Combining these terms, the final weight matrix 𝐖 C \mathbf{W}_{C} is computed as: 𝐖 C = γ ~ 0 ​ 𝐖 0 + β ~ 0 ​ R 1 ​ 𝐌 0 + ∑ t = 1 C ( η t ​ β ~ t ​ R t ) ​ 𝐆 t . \mathbf{W}_{C}=\tilde{\gamma}_{0}\mathbf{W}_{0}\,+\,\tilde{\beta}_{0}R_{1}\mathbf{M}_{0}\,+\,\sum_{t=1}^{C}\big(\eta_{t}\,\tilde{\beta}_{t}\,R_{t}\big)\,\mathbf{G}_{t}. (30) Closed form for 𝐌 C \mathbf{M}_{C} . The momentum recurrence is uncoupled from 𝐖 t \mathbf{W}_{t} , so its closed form follows directly from ( 18 ) by setting t = C t=C : 𝐌 C = ( ∏ i = 1 C β i ) ​ 𝐌 0 + ∑ t = 1 C ( η t ​ 𝐆 t ​ ∏ i = t + 1 C β i ) . \mathbf{M}_{C}=\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{C}\beta_{i}\Big)\mathbf{M}_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{C}\Big(\eta_{t}\,\mathbf{G}_{t}\prod_{i=t+1}^{C}\beta_{i}\Big). (31) Recognizing the suffix products defined in ( 23 ), β ~ 0 = ∏ i = 1 C β i \tilde{\beta}_{0}=\prod_{i=1}^{C}\beta_{i} and β ~ t = ∏ i = t + 1 C β i \tilde{\beta}_{t}=\prod_{i=t+1}^{C}\beta_{i} , Eq. ( 31 ) collapses to the parallel kernel form 𝐌 C = β ~ 0 ​ 𝐌 0 + ∑ t = 1 C ( η t ​ β ~ t ) ​ 𝐆 t . \mathbf{M}_{C}=\tilde{\beta}_{0}\,\mathbf{M}_{0}\,+\,\sum_{t=1}^{C}\big(\eta_{t}\,\tilde{\beta}_{t}\big)\,\mathbf{G}_{t}. (32) Unlike 𝐖 C \mathbf{W}_{C} , the momentum kernel involves no cumulative ratio R t R_{t} : each gradient 𝐆 t \mathbf{G}_{t} is propagated to the chunk end through a single suffix product β ~ t \tilde{\beta}_{t} , since only one decay channel ( β \beta ) acts on 𝐌 t \mathbf{M}_{t} . This formulation allows us to “jump” directly from t = 0 t=0 to t = C t=C without materializing intermediate states. sections.text: Within a chunk, all gradients 𝐆 t \mathbf{G}_{t} in our formulation are evaluated at the frozen 𝐖 0 \mathbf{W}_{0} (Sec. 3.2 ). Under this constraint, the closed-form chunk-end states from Proposition 3.1 admit two complementary readings. Optimization-style view. Equation ( 7 ) reads as a token-wise state recurrence with momentum factor β t \beta_{t} and L 2 decay factor γ t \gamma_{t} , both modulated per token. This is the framing we adopt throughout the paper, for consistency with the mini-batch and chunk-wise TTT literature [ 56 , 9 , 69 ] . It is genuinely descriptive at the inter-chunk level: 𝐌 C \mathbf{M}_{C} is carried into the next chunk and accumulates momentum over the full sequence. Kernel-weighting view. Equivalently, the chunk-end states can be read as scalar-weighted aggregations of per-token gradients, 𝐖 C = γ ~ 0 ​ 𝐖 0 + β ~ 0 ​ R 1 ​ 𝐌 0 + ∑ t = 1 C 𝒦 t W ​ 𝐆 t , 𝐌 C = β ~ 0 ​ 𝐌 0 + ∑ t = 1 C 𝒦 t M ​ 𝐆 t , \mathbf{W}_{C}\;=\;\tilde{\gamma}_{0}\mathbf{W}_{0}+\tilde{\beta}_{0}R_{1}\mathbf{M}_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{C}\mathcal{K}^{W}_{t}\,\mathbf{G}_{t},\qquad\mathbf{M}_{C}\;=\;\tilde{\beta}_{0}\mathbf{M}_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{C}\mathcal{K}^{M}_{t}\,\mathbf{G}_{t}, in which ( 𝒦 t W , 𝒦 t M ) (\mathcal{K}^{W}_{t},\mathcal{K}^{M}_{t}) act as learned, time-aware kernel weights over per-token gradient contributions to the chunk-end states. sections.heading: B.2 Evaluation Details
sections.text: Commonsense Reasoning. Following prior work [ 21 , 64 , 28 ] , we evaluate our model on multiple commonsense reasoning benchmarks: PIQA [ 10 ] , HellaSwag [ 68 , Hella.;] , WinoGrande [ 53 , Wino.;] , ARC-easy (ARC-e) and ARC-challenge (ARC-c) [ 11 ] , Wikitext [ 40 , Wiki.;] , and LAMBADA [ 45 , LMB.;] . All evaluations are performed using lm-evaluation-harness [ 18 ] . In-context Retrieval. Following prior work [ 66 , 5 , 28 ] , we focus on three tasks: FDA [ 5 ] , SWDE [ 38 ] , and SQuAD [ 51 ] . For SQuAD and SWDE, we use lm-evaluation-harness [ 18 ] for evaluation. For FDA, we follow Irie et al. [28] and use the evaluation script from Arora et al. [4] . Length Extrapolation. We first assess whether the models can maintain stable language modeling performance when processing sequences longer than their training context (2K tokens). Following Yang et al. [64] , we conduct experiments on six diverse long-context benchmarks: PG19 [ 50 ] , GovReport [ 27 ] , QMSum [ 71 ] , NarrativeQA [ 33 ] , Qasper [ 14 ] , and CodeParrot. To test effective capacity, we utilize the S-NIAH-1 (passkey retrieval) and S-NIAH-2 (numerical needle in haystack) tasks from RULER’s Needle-In-A-Haystack Single (NIAH-S) benchmark suite [ 24 ] . Finally, we evaluate on 14 real-world long-context tasks from Longbench [ 7 ] , including: narrative comprehension (Narrative QA [ 33 ] ), scientific understanding (QasperQA [ 14 ] ), multi-hop reasoning (MultiField QA, HotpotQA [ 67 ] , 2WikiMulti QA [ 23 ] , Musique [ 60 ] ), document summarization (GovReport [ 27 ] , QMSum [ 71 ] , MultiNews [ 17 ] ), and various specialized tasks (TRec [ 35 ] , Trivia QA [ 29 ] , SamSum [ 19 ] , LCC [ 22 ] , and RepoBench-P [ 37 ] ). All evaluations, except for the stability analysis, are performed using lm-evaluation-harness [ 18 ] . Video Understanding. We evaluate on two standard video understanding benchmarks: VideoMMMU [ 25 ] and LongVideoBench [ 62 ] . Following the Qwen3VL [ 6 ] protocol, we employ a uniform sampling strategy to extract a fixed sequence of frames from each video. We configure the frame count and token budget to balance temporal range with spatial resolution: for VideoMMMU, we sample 512 frames with a maximum of 256 tokens per frame, and for LongVideoBench, 256 frames with 512 tokens. Hybrid Baselines. We benchmark against two competitive hybrid architectures: HQLT [ 28 ] and LaCT [ 69 ] . For HQLT, which combines DeltaNet [ 54 ] with window attention, we select the synchronous variant where both components process inputs simultaneously; this configuration is reported as the optimal setting by the authors. For LaCT, which fuses chunk-wise TTT (parameterized by a SwiGLU MLP) with window attention, we evaluate the variant utilizing Muon optimization for the TTT update rule, consistent with the best-performing configuration provided in the official implementation.

To validate the hardware efficiency of our proposed method, we evaluate training throughput (measured in kilo-tokens per second, kTPS) and utilization (TFLOPS) on a single H100 64GB GPU. We test two model scales (340M and 1.3B parameters) on 2K sequences, using batch sizes of 4 and 2, respectively. We compare E 2 -TTT against Titans [ 9 ] and LaCT [ 69 ] . All baselines are implemented in PyTorch under identical training conditions. As no official Titans implementation was available at the time of writing, we report a self-reproduction following the architecture described in Behrouz et al. [9] ; we implemented both the scan-based formulation and the memory-optimized dual form [ 56 ] and report the latter, which we found slightly faster in PyTorch. As shown in Figure 5 , Titans is severely throughput-bound: at 340M it achieves less than 2 kTPS, and at 1.3B it goes out-of-memory. This is consistent with the structure of the dual form for nonlinear inner models such as TTT-MLP: each inner-model layer is reformulated as a masked attention-like computation (Appendix A.3, Sun et al. [56] ), and this machinery lies on the outer-loop autograd path, inflating both activation memory and backward-pass cost. The dual form does eliminate per-token state materialization in principle, but for TTT-MLP the small inner mini-batch size (64 in our setting) combined with these masked-matmul overheads dominates throughput. These costs are absent under chunk-wise output (Eq. 6 ), where the per-chunk forward and backward operate on a single fast-weight state. In contrast, both E 2 -TTT variants stay close to the throughput of the highly optimized LaCT baseline despite computing the exact closed-form kernel rather than a single averaged factor. The additional bookkeeping incurred by our kernel—log-space suffix products, ratio sums, and a scalar re-weighting that yields 𝐌 C \mathbf{M}_{C} from the same backward pass that produces 𝐖 C \mathbf{W}_{C} —is cheap relative to the fast-weight forward and backward themselves. sections.heading: Impact Statement and Limitations
sections.text: E 2 -TTT advances the efficiency of long-context sequence modeling by parallelizing token-wise Test-Time Training updates. As a foundational architecture for general-purpose language and multimodal models, it inherits the broad set of societal considerations associated with such models, but does not introduce risks specific to the proposed mechanism beyond those already present in existing TTT and linear-attention variants. We highlight two limitations of the current study. First, the chunk-wise output step (Eq. 6 ) applies a fixed fast-weight state to all tokens within a chunk, producing a within-chunk “blind spot” for fine-grained causal dependencies; we mitigate this in practice through the sliding-window attention branch, and developing an efficient token-wise output step remains an interesting direction for future work. Second, following the standard evaluation protocol of recent TTT and linear-attention work [ 56 , 28 ] , our experiments are conducted at scales up to 1.3B parameters; extending E 2 -TTT to larger model sizes is a natural direction for future work.

We propose E 2 -TTT (Expressive and Efficient TTT) to bridge this gap. Under the standard approximation of taking gradients at the chunk-start weights, we derive a closed-form state transition that exactly reproduces the chunk-end fast-weight and momentum states of the per-token recurrence. This enables fully parallelized chunk-level training while preserving the temporal structure of the update rule that prior chunk-wise methods discard. We validate E 2 -TTT by training models up to 1.3B parameters from scratch. It performs on par with previous TTT and hybrid attention baselines in language modeling while outperforming them on in-context retrieval. Its advantage is most pronounced in length extrapolation: on the standard “Needle in a Haystack” passkey test, it retains over 90% accuracy at 8 × 8	imes the training context length. Meanwhile, E 2 -TTT can match the training throughput of efficient chunk-wise methods, demonstrating that it effectively reconciles expressivity with efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/zeyun-zhong/E2-TTT . 1 Introduction State-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) [ 44 , 16 , 2 ] demonstrate remarkable capabilities in reasoning, coding, and multimodal understanding. However, once trained, the weights of these models remain frozen, leaving them to rely solely on accumulated memory, e.g. , key-value cache [ 48 , 49 ] , for processing long-context agentic tasks [ 43 , 41 , 34 ] . This fundamental limitation hinders their ability to continuously learn from long-horizon tasks or generalize across tasks in real-world scenarios. Two primary approaches have emerged to address this limitation. The first seeks to reduce the computational complexity of attention from quadratic to linear by introducing RNN-style or hybrid architectures [ 13 , 64 , 47 , 32 ] , thereby enabling the processing of longer sequences. However, as demonstrated in Tandon et al. [58] , these techniques still remain less effective than full attention in long-context language modeling. The second approach, known as Test-Time Training [ 56 , 9 ] , extends the concept of recurrent states to small, online-adapted sub-networks ( e.g. , fast weights [ 54 ] ), allowing models to continuously adapt their parameters during inference. Numerous recent studies [ 12 , 58 , 69 ] have explored its potential for long-context text and multimodal tasks. Despite their promise, existing TTT methods face a well-known dilemma between expressivity and efficiency. On the one hand, vanilla TTT [ 56 , 9 ] adopts token-wise updates, which offer powerful expressiveness but result in slow training, as token-level dependencies enforce sequential recurrence. On the other hand, chunk-wise TTT [ 69 ] substantially improves efficiency by executing updates over larger chunks, yet it sacrifices expressivity due to oversimplifications of the update rule, effectively obscuring the temporal variance of token importance within a chunk. To achieve the best of both worlds in expressivity and efficiency, we propose E 2 -TTT, a novel TTT approach that reconciles token-level expressiveness with chunk-level computational efficiency. The core innovation is a closed-form parallel scalar kernel that enables parallel execution of recurrent dynamics with per-token learning rate, momentum, and decay. Specifically, our formulation preserves the exact per-token effect on the chunk-end fast-weight state, a temporal structure that prior chunk-wise methods discard via averaging, while retaining chunk-level hardware parallelism. Furthermore, we integrate E 2 -TTT into a hybrid architecture that combines TTT with sliding window attention, enabling our model to handle long-horizon tasks while maintaining fine-grained local context. We empirically validate E 2 -TTT by training models of up to 1.3B parameters from scratch on 15B tokens from the HuggingFace FineWeb-Edu dataset [ 46 ] , comparing against strong linear attention and hybrid baselines. Our evaluation spans general language modeling, in-context retrieval, and length extrapolation, where the gains concentrate in the retrieval and extrapolation regimes. Notably, our model exhibits strong robustness in length extrapolation, maintaining > 90 % >90\% accuracy on passkey retrieval in the standard “Needle in a Haystack” test at 8 × 8	imes the training context, a regime where prior chunk-based methods collapse. Finally, we explore the versatility of our approach through parameter-efficient adaptation for long-context video understanding, achieving performance comparable to full fine-tuning at the 2B-parameter scale on standard multimodal benchmarks. Overall Architecture. The macro-architecture of E 2 -TTT follows the standard Llama design [ 59 ] , interleaving token mixing layers with SwiGLU MLP blocks. Given an input sequence 𝐗 ∈ ℝ L × d \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{L	imes d} , we first project it into shared queries 𝐐 \mathbf{Q} , keys 𝐊 \mathbf{K} , and values 𝐕 \mathbf{V} .
